description: Tungsten is a chemical element with symbol W and atomic number 74, a metal found naturally on Earth almost exclusively in compounds with other elements. It was identified as a distinct element in 1781 and first isolated as a metal in 1783. Its important ores include scheelite and wolframite.
uses: Tungsten occurs in many alloys with numerous applications including incandescent light bulb filaments, X-ray tubes, electrodes in gas tungsten arc welding, superalloys, and radiation shielding. Its largest use is in tungsten carbide, a wear-resistant material used in metalworking, mining, and construction. Tungsten compounds are used as industrial catalysts and its hardness and high density make it suitable for military applications in penetrating projectiles.
characteristics: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all known elements at 3,422 °C and the highest boiling point at 5,930 °C, with a density of 19.254 g/cm³. Polycrystalline tungsten is an intrinsically brittle and hard material, though pure single-crystalline tungsten is more ductile. It is a mostly non-reactive element that does not react with water, most acids and bases, or oxygen at room temperature, but reacts directly with fluorine at room temperature.
